title: Can four be worth more than seven?

audience.curriculum: Primary decimal place value; curriculum certification not assessed

learningContract.objective: Explain why the 4 in 3.47 contributes more than the 7, using tenths and hundredths of the same whole.
prerequisites: Recognise equal parts of a whole
misconceptions: A larger digit always contributes a larger value
One tenth and one hundredth are the same size
Subdividing a whole increases its quantity
learningContract.successEvidence: The learner explains that four tenths equal forty hundredths, which exceed seven hundredths, then distinguishes the 6 in 0.6 from the 6 in 0.06.
learningContract.prerequisiteResponse: If equal partitioning or counting in tens is unfamiliar, teach those prerequisites first; this fixed video cannot diagnose or adapt automatically.

invariants: The square keeps the same boundary, position and size
All hundredth cells have equal area
Partitioning changes the description, not the amount
Colour is supported by words and position, never the only cue
representation.rationale: A fixed area model makes the ten-to-one relationship visible. A place-value chart alone names columns without demonstrating their relative quantities.
rejectedAlternatives: Unconnected enlarged tiles obscure the unit
A moving camera competes with inspecting equal parts

sources.title: EEF mathematics recommendations
sources.use: Prior knowledge, purposeful representations, misconceptions, worked examples and explaining reasoning; not validation of this video

beats.title: Can four be worth more than seven?
beats.learnerQuestion: Does the larger digit always contribute more?
beats.action: Invite a prediction without revealing the answer
beats.text: Seven is a bigger digit than four. But in three point four seven, which digit contributes more? Make a prediction. Let's find out why.

beats.title: First, agree on one whole
beats.learnerQuestion: What quantity are our parts measured against?
beats.action: Reveal one square at its permanent size and position
beats.text: This square represents one whole. Keep its outside edge in view. We will divide it into equal parts, without making the whole any bigger.

beats.title: Ten equal parts make tenths
beats.learnerQuestion: What is one of ten equal parts?
beats.action: Draw nine vertical dividers, then highlight exactly one strip
beats.endState: Ten equal strips with one selected
beats.text: Divide the square into ten equal strips. One strip is one of ten equal parts. We call it one tenth, and write zero point one.

beats.title: Notice what has stayed the same
beats.learnerQuestion: Did dividing make the whole larger?
beats.startState: Ten strips inside the unchanged boundary
beats.action: Hold the whole and the highlighted strip still for inspection
beats.endState: The same whole; only its partition has changed
beats.text: Notice that the whole has not grown. Only the lines have changed. All ten strips together still make exactly one whole.

beats.title: Look inside one tenth
beats.learnerQuestion: How many smaller equal parts fit inside one tenth?
beats.action: Draw nine short dividers inside that strip, then extend them across the other strips
beats.endState: Ten rows and ten columns inside the original whole
beats.text: Now split this one strip into ten equal pieces. There are ten little pieces in each strip. Across all ten strips, that makes one hundred equal pieces.

beats.title: One tenth is ten hundredths
beats.learnerQuestion: How are the two units related?
beats.startState: The complete hundred-square with one tenth selected
beats.action: Count the ten cells of the selected strip without changing its area
beats.endState: The same strip explicitly mapped to ten hundredths
beats.text: Each little piece is one hundredth of the whole. Count the ten pieces in our highlighted strip. One tenth is the same amount as ten hundredths.

beats.title: Build the value of the four
beats.learnerQuestion: How much do four tenths represent?
beats.startState: One tenth represented by ten hundredths
beats.action: Highlight four complete columns in order and count ten, twenty, thirty, forty
beats.endState: Forty equal cells shaded; notation 4 tenths = 40 hundredths = 0.4
beats.text: Let's build four tenths. One strip, two, three, four. Counting the small pieces gives ten, twenty, thirty, forty. So four tenths equal forty hundredths: zero point four.

beats.title: Build the value of the seven
beats.action: Add seven individual equal cells in the next column, leaving the forty cells intact
beats.endState: Four tenths and seven hundredths shown on the same whole
beats.text: The seven is in the hundredths place. Add seven little pieces beside our four strips. Seven hundredths is zero point zero seven. It does not fill even one tenth.

beats.title: Compare using the same-sized pieces
beats.learnerQuestion: Why does the four contribute more?
beats.startState: Forty teal cells and seven rust cells in the same grid
beats.action: Outline each contribution and reveal a forty-versus-seven comparison
beats.endState: A visual and numerical explanation of 0.4 > 0.07
beats.text: Now compare the same-sized pieces. Forty hundredths are more than seven hundredths. So the four contributes more, even though four is the smaller digit. Its place makes the difference.

beats.title: Put the explanation back into 3.47
beats.learnerQuestion: How does the model connect to the written number?
beats.action: Link the model to the tenths and hundredths digits; keep the three ones as written context
beats.text: In three point four seven, the three contributes three wholes. The four contributes four tenths, and the seven contributes seven hundredths. The square shows just the fractional part.

beats.title: Your turn: explain the three
beats.learnerQuestion: Can the learner identify a new digit contribution?
beats.startState: A new number, 2.63, without labels or shaded quantities
beats.action: Show only the number and question; hold all answers out of every visible layer
beats.endState: The learner has time to state a value and reason
beats.text: Your turn. In two point six three, what value does the three contribute? Say the value and explain how its place tells you. Pause the video if you need longer.

assessment.expected: Three hundredths, or 0.03, because 3 is in the second place after the decimal point

beats.title: The three contributes three hundredths
beats.action: Reveal the two fractional column labels and a three-cell model only after the thinking pause
beats.endState: 3 hundredths = 0.03, linked to the second decimal place
beats.text: The three is in the hundredths place, the second place after the decimal point. It contributes three hundredths: zero point zero three. Three small pieces of a hundred-square show that amount.

beats.title: Same digit. Same value?
beats.learnerQuestion: Does the learner understand place rather than memorising a digit?
beats.action: Present both numbers without models, labels or an inequality
beats.text: One last puzzle. Compare zero point six and zero point zero six. Both use the digit six. Does the six have the same value? Explain your answer before we check.

assessment.expected: No: six tenths equal sixty hundredths; six hundredths are smaller
wrongAnswers: Same value: attending only to the digit
0.06 is larger: treating decimals as whole-number strings

beats.title: Six tenths is sixty hundredths
beats.learnerQuestion: Can the representation justify the new comparison?
beats.action: Reveal two equal-sized hundred-squares: sixty cells versus six, then label their values
beats.text: No. In zero point six, the six means six tenths: sixty hundredths. In zero point zero six, it means six hundredths. Sixty pieces are more than six, when every piece is the same size.

beats.title: Read the place, then name the value
beats.learnerQuestion: What reusable explanation should the child retain?
beats.startState: The transfer comparison and equal-unit models
beats.action: Hold the evidence while revealing the general rule
beats.endState: A digit's place determines its contribution
beats.text: A digit tells us how many units. Its place tells us which units. When you explain a decimal, name both: how many, and tenths or hundredths.

checksRequired: All visible layers during question and pause
Human listening and educator review before claiming teaching quality

childTestProtocol.before: Ask which contributes more, the 2 or the 8 in 1.28, and record the explanation without correcting it
childTestProtocol.after: Ask which contributes more, the 3 or the 9 in 2.39, and why; then ask about 0.5 versus 0.05
childTestProtocol.interpretation: Use individual explanations to revise the lesson. A small informal pilot does not establish causal learning gains or age-wide effectiveness.
